transcript.content: Hi, welcome in. I'm Dr. Lee. To start, can you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

I’m here because I can’t stop noticing this rough, sunken-looking patch on my face. In pictures and in the mirror, one side looks old and beat-up to me. Other people tell me they hardly see anything, but I see it all the time.

When people tell you they don't notice anything unusual about your skin, is there any part of you that considers they might be right, or are you completely certain that the flaw is really there exactly as you see it?

I mean, I hear them, but it’s hard for me to believe it. When I look in the mirror or see a photo, that patch looks rough and sunken to me—like that side of my face looks old and beat-up. I can’t seem to stop seeing it.

Aside from your concerns about this patch on your face, have you noticed any other unusual beliefs or experiences lately—like feeling that people are watching or talking about you, or hearing or sensing things that others don't?
No, I haven’t noticed anything like that. It’s really just the concern about my face.

Do you find yourself doing things like checking the patch in mirrors repeatedly, trying to cover or camouflage it with makeup or your hand, picking at the skin there, or asking others for reassurance about how it looks?

Yeah. Before work, or if I’m going to my sister’s game night, I can stand in the bathroom checking it over and over, turning my face under different lights. I rub at the spot too. Sometimes I pull a hat down low, or I just make up an excuse not to go if it looks too obvious to me.

If I showed you a photo of your face alongside photos of several other people, and asked you to point out which face had the flaw you're describing, how confident are you that you could convince a neutral stranger who has no stake in the matter that the patch is really there the way you see it?

I’d be pretty confident. I mean, in a photo I can see that rough, sunken area right away—it makes that side of my face look older, beat-up. Other people say they barely notice it, but I don’t see how they couldn’t if they really looked.
If you really try, is there any small percentage chance, even just 1%, that this patch might look far less noticeable than you believe, or that your perception could be off?

I guess there’s always some tiny chance, but it doesn’t feel that way to me. I see it in the mirror and in photos—that rough, sunken patch—and it makes that side of my face look old and beat-up. People say they barely notice it, but I honestly don’t understand how.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient demonstrates a persistent, distressing preoccupation with a perceived flaw (a rough, sunken patch on the face) that is not observable or appears only slight to others, consistent with Body Dysmorphic Disorder. The preoccupation is accompanied by repetitive behaviors (mirror checking, camouflaging with hats, rubbing/picking at the skin, avoidance of social situations) aimed at addressing the perceived defect, fulfilling core BDD criteria. Insight is poor—the patient acknowledges only a minimal (1%) possibility that their perception is inaccurate, but does not hold a fixed, unshakeable delusional belief, and no other psychotic symptoms (hallucinations, paranoia) are present, arguing against Delusional Disorder, Somatic Type (F22). The behaviors are specifically tied to appearance concerns rather than general contamination, symmetry, or intrusive thoughts unrelated to appearance, differentiating this from OCD (F42).
